or one's entire wealth, or half of that, or half of that again, according to his command."
If power (*śakti*) were not mobile, how could it belong to him?
Also in the *Nīlatantra*:
"By the mere satisfaction of the Guru, eternal accomplishment (*siddhi*) comes to pass."
Otherwise, there would be no accomplishment at all; it serves only for malevolent magic.
One should give as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) one's entire wealth— cows, gold, garments, and so forth— according to one's capacity, and one should also give cows that yield milk.
One should grant land that provides a livelihood, which shall follow one's sons and grandsons.
In the *Phetkārīya*: "One should give a teacher a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of gold accompanied by a garment."
By the mere satisfaction of the Guru, eternal perfection is attained.
Otherwise, there would be no success at all; it leads only to malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). One should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins preceded by great respect.
Such is the distinction. In the *Nīlatantra* and the *Matasūkta*, it is stated:
"In this matter, even that which is not contradictory [to other scriptures] should be performed. Likewise, in the *Svatantratantra*:
"One should follow its shadow and dwell nearby for three days."
If this mobile power does not reach the Guru, there is no doubt [of success].
On whichever day one obtains this mantra, there shall be gain therein;
the reversal of both good and evil karmas becomes certain.
Thus ends the second chapter, the rule for initiation.
Now begins the third chapter:
Thus, having received initiation from a true guru, one should commence the *puraścaraṇa* for the sake of attaining success in the mantra. Likewise, in the *Nīlatantra*:
Just as a body devoid of life is incapable of performing any action,
so too is a mantra proclaimed to be ineffective when it lacks the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
Recitation, fire-oblation, libation, sprinkling, and the feeding of Brahmins—
this fivefold rite is indeed called *puraścaraṇa* in this world.

In this context, among the five limbs [of the ritual], the primary importance belongs to the recitation (*japa*). The other four should be understood as being subordinate to it, because they are prescribed as its auxiliaries once that [recitation] has been accomplished. As stated in the *Gāndharva*:
"Having performed it in this manner, one who eats sacrificial food and whose mind is focused on nothing else should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times."
Then, one should perform the ritual application for all [rites], such as those for subjugation and so forth.
There is also a specific rule in the Vīra-tantra: "A practitioner of mantra, intent on acting according to his own will,
should always recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while holding a secret rosary for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa)."
42) It should be repeated: "Even if one is dull-witted or mute, if one is intent upon the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*),"
One obtains the speech of the illustrious through one hundred thousand recitations of the mantra.

For it has been stated that "the wise, having relied upon the words of the illustrious Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, and others, composed the Mahābhārata and other works. In this context, however, they prescribe a fourfold repetition for those who are capable of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and who abstain from various worldly activities. As it is said in the *Ekavīratantra*:
But for those who are devoid of meditation, who are petty and of small minds, it is said that the recitation must be fourfold for success; otherwise, it will not come to pass.

Thus, even for Brahmins and others who are unable to perform the Mahācīna-krama, the recitation (japa) should be performed according to the fourfold rule. For it is heard [in scripture]: "Even one who is dull-witted, if he should be mute, he becomes intent upon the power of meditative visualization (bhāvanā).
Furthermore, elsewhere:
All castes, including the twice-born, are devoted to the secret path;
yet all castes, individually and separately, remain detached from its practice.

In this regard, for those who have mastered the vidyā through the conduct as previously described, there is no need for the exertion of fourfold service during the age (yuga). As it is stated in the Phetkārīya:
"Especially in the Kali age, [this] shall come to pass through my grace."
Since this mantra is already perfected even in the *Matysasūkta*, there is no need for the exertion of worshiping it through the four ages (*yuga-sevā*).
Regarding the conduct during the period of preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), he says:
Eating only at night, pure and consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should recite the vidyā during the day;
having performed that, one attains success, and should recite it with a steady mind.
And so it has been said by the venerable Gūḍhapāda:
"Sleeping on the ground, restraint of speech, abstention from women, rising at dawn, [offering] branches and fuel, and the purification of teeth and tongue."
In the leaf-plate was sweet food; with the flowers of the Brahma-tree were performed worship and fire-offerings; and there were radiant garlands, drinks, and ointments.
During the time of mantra recitation, one should always carefully avoid one's wife;
one should avoid the Viṣṇukalpa plant and avoid a Tulasī leaf.
One should avoid the *mālatī* flower and avoid other forms of worship;
having rinsed the hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should perform each of those [acts] with purity.
And likewise, one should assign separate vessels for the flowers of the goddesses.
If one desires success for oneself, one should not treat [the deity] as a single entity;
one should know that [the deity] partakes of the offerings, fruits, water, and so forth.
One should offer oblations with various kinds of fragrances, milk-rice, sweetmeats, and so forth;
likewise, one should employ curd and milk in this same sequence.
As stated in the *Phetkārīya*:
"If one suddenly desires success by means of the rosary called the Great Conch (*mahāśaṅkha*),
a rosary fashioned from fifty beads bestows all accomplishments."

The mantra of Mahāśaṅkha Nīlasarasvatī yields its fruit quickly. In the absence of a human forehead bone, a substitute may be used for the sake of practicality; the bone of another body may also be taken. Thus says the commentary within the Śaiva Dīkṣā. Now, the consecration of the rosary (mālā-saṃskāra) is as follows, according to the Ekavīrā Kalpa.
Whether it be sewn or knotted, made from the thread of a twice-born woman's garment,
one should join mouth to mouth and tail to tail.
One should have the *mātṛkā* knots made according to the number of syllables, either in the shape of a snake, or like a cow's tail, or by means of a *vidyā*.
Then, one should fashion a single bead of that same kind as Mount Meru;
thus strung, this garland bestows the accomplishment of mantras.
On an auspicious ascendant, under a favorable weekday, in a favorable lunar mansion, and on a favorable lunar day,
the mantra-practitioner should perform the consecration, either by himself or through a preceptor.
One should fashion a nine-petaled *āśvattha* leaf in the shape of a lotus;
there, the practitioner of mantra, reciting the *mātṛkā* mantra, should establish [the deity].
Having consecrated the fire according to the rules, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations;
one should present the remainder of the oblations as a pleasing offering for each deity during the counter-oblation.
There, having worshipped the Goddess, one should also worship the planetary deities;
one should consecrate them with the syllables of the Mātṛkā, both in direct and reverse order.
Having consulted with the preta regarding Meru, one should meditate upon it as being of the nature of the deity;
thus, endowed with all virtues, it arises for the sake of all accomplishments.
As it is said in the Śāmbhavīya:
"The thread is sewn, the Vītihotra [fire] is established, and again there is a double revolution;
day and night are declared to be the two [other fires]; therefore, the triad of lights is auspicious."
He who performs the supreme recitation with such a rosary made of akṣa seeds, [attains the highest merit].
One is liberated from untimely death and the Kali age; of this there is no doubt.
One should mutter [the mantra] day and night, keeping it secret, for the attainment of one's desired goal.

The determination of the *karamālā* (rosary of the hand) is as follows. It is stated in the *Haṃsapārameśvara*: "One should rotate the two joints of the ring finger in sequence; one should take three joints of the middle finger and one joint of the index finger."
Now, regarding the fault of leaping over Mount Meru:
it has been declared that the *Śaktimālā* is the illuminator of all mantras;
yet, whatever is recited here with a distracted mind, or whatever is recited by leaping over Mount Meru, [is fruitless].
"O Supreme Goddess, all that [practice] becomes fruitless; know this to be the command, O Pārvatī. Furthermore, O Pārvatī, understand that the Meru is formed by the two joints of the index finger."
For the sake of accomplishment, the practitioner should recite [the mantra] over Mount Meru, bowing again and again;
likewise, he who recites it with the tip of the index finger or the middle finger is also a doer of evil.
As it is said in the *Ekavīrātantra*: "Then, having bowed to Kullukā and performed the worship of the rosary, one should take hold of it with the right hand; one must not touch it with the left."
One should contemplate the *kullukā* at the region of the head from the navel;
this rosary, composed by Bhaṭṭasūtrakṛt, is always pleasing to the Goddess.
Alternatively, in the absence of a great conch-shell, one may perform the recitation with a rosary made of fifty gems, such as crystal and so forth.
Now, the most secret of secrets regarding the rosary for supreme yogis is written down. As it is stated in the Viśuddheśvara Tantra:
45) O Pārvatī, listen now to the supreme method for the rosary according to its true nature;
by the mere knowledge of which, mantras are accomplished in that very instant.
By means of the mere mantra in both direct and reverse order,
one should intersperse the letters with the mantra and the mantra with the letters.
One should fashion a garland made of letters that illuminates all mantras;
one must never transgress the final letter, which has the form of Mount Meru.
"As Meru is the head of all [mountains] and as I, Hari, am among the gods, so it is.
(From the *Matsyasūkta*) Therefore, with a steady mind, one should perform action day and night.
This supreme secret has been told to you by me, O illustrious lady.
You must act with extreme secrecy; this must not be told to anyone at all.

Then, for the sake of accomplishment, always adopting devotion to the Guru, facing north and meditating on the *kullukā* upon one's head, one should recite [the mantra] according to the prescribed number. As it is said in the *Phetkārīya*:
"With a state of constant devotion toward the lotus-feet of the Guru..."
He serves obediently and becomes devoted to him with his whole being; honoring him day after day,
that man becomes a proponent in this world who destroys the doctrine of duality.
And so it is said in the Matsya Purāṇa: "If a man does not know the *kullukā* and yet mutters the great mantra, he must continue muttering it for as long as he lives; it will never be perfected."
He who abandons the great mantra and worships Tāriṇī instead will meet his death or become insane.
The wise man among the twice-born should never fail to worship the mantra of Tāriṇī and Caṇḍikā, excluding the *kulluka*.
And by wearing the *kullukā* on the head, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
Also in the Māyātantra:
"One should wear the *kullukā* on the head, having written it upon a birch-bark leaf.
In the assembly hall and at the royal gate, one certainly becomes victorious;
there is no other consideration anywhere—this is the view approved by Virūpākṣa.
If the *kulluka* is excluded from men's sacrifices, there shall be no participation;
my worship will always be in vain, and likewise my sacrifice.
That fool who does not know the supreme three-syllabled general mantra of Tārā should not worship the captivating Kullukā.
Even if one recites it for as long as one lives, it will never be accomplished;
for he who abandons the Great Mantra and worships Tāriṇī instead.
He meets his death or becomes insane;
that goddess named Kullukā is the embodiment of spiritual power.
Holding a bow in her hand, endowed with four arms,
her body dark like a blue lotus, and adorned with all ornaments.
One should write the three-syllable mantra with either turmeric or sandalwood paste and always wear it on the crest-lock for as long as one lives, without indolence.

"Having attained [the state] through the great Vidyā, one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times. Thus, the previously mentioned locations and other details are to be observed. Having recited it in the manner described, one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), consecration (*abhiṣeka*), feeding of Brahmins, and the offering of fees to the preceptor (*gurudakṣiṇā*) in one-tenth of that number. As it has been said:
One should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times while consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya) and with senses subdued,
staying in the aforementioned locations and established upon their respective seats.
Having performed the previously mentioned worship and being intent upon honoring the Brahmins,
one should thereafter perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites in sequence, using a tenth part [of the materials].
The *bali* offering should always be given at night by those desiring all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*), however, should be performed with blue lotuses or *bilva* leaves. This has been stated in the *Siddhasārasvata*:

Having thus performed the recitation, the practitioner of mantra should offer oblations with blue lotuses smeared with clarified butter amounting to one-tenth of that number, and should satisfy [the deity] with one-tenth of that amount.
One should satisfy that supreme goddess with pure perfumed waters mixed with liquid black aloe-wood; the method for doing so is stated here.
Having invoked [the goddess] into the water according to the rules with water for the feet and other offerings,
and having worshipped the Goddess and her retinue according to the rules, once each;
Having gratified [the deity] according to the rules with devotion, one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) ten times that amount;
then, having gratified each one again, one should likewise gratify the retinue.
Then one should perform the consecration; hear from me its procedure.
Having worshipped his own self with the thought that it is the Goddess, the best of practitioners—
Thinking, "I shall sprinkle Tāriṇī," one should project the syllable *namaḥ* upon the head;
this is declared to be the consecration that cuts through all sins.
The feeding of the practitioners should be done with a tenth part of the offerings for the consecration;
immediately after that, one should feed the resident female disciple and the young maiden.
Through foods consisting of milk, sugar-candy, and ghee, the accomplishment of the mantra will certainly occur;
one should give a sacrificial fee to the Guru preceded by great respect.

Thus it is stated in the *Nīlatārātantra*. Also, in the *Urdhvāmnāya*: "At the end of the mantra, having uttered the name, one should say 'svāhā' for the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and 'namaḥ' for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and worship (*pūjana*); thereafter, one says 'I satisfy' (*tarpayāmi*)."
At the end of "svāhā," there should be the act of satiation; now hear from me regarding the consecration.
Having uttered the name at the end of the mantra, I shall then perform the sprinkling.
One should provide food for one-tenth of that number of Brahmins;
thus, having attained mastery over the mantra, one shall accomplish all desires.
Also in the *Matsya-sūkta*:

"Then one should offer unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and bilva leaves ten times [the number of oblations]. Only sesame and clarified butter," say the great teachers. And one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*guru*). Likewise:
Without knowing the *kullukā*, without having worshipped the Goddess,
without properly giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and without performing the sequential worship (*kramapūjana*);
"Whoever engages in this mantra, you certainly afflict him"—from such statements in the *Matsyasūkta*. Thus ends the third chapter, the Determination of the Puraścaraṇa.
The Fourth Chapter:
Now, the performance of occasional rites (*naimittika-anuṣṭhāna*). As it is stated in the *Svatantra-tantra*:
"The obligatory (*nitya*), the occasional (*naimittika*), and the optional (*kāmya*) [rites] depend upon each other, each preceding one being more fundamental than the next."
If it were otherwise, one would incur a succession of calamities by acting in this manner.
In the *Nīlatantra*:

"The practitioner of mantra, devoted to the daily worship (*nityārcana*), should perform the occasional worship (*naimittikārcana*). Once the occasional worship is accomplished, he may perform the optional worship (*kāmya*) even if it is incomplete."
As it is said in the Matsyasūkta:
"On the eighth and the fourteenth [lunar days], one should worship with great effort;
whatever the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) desires, that he shall obtain constantly."
One obtains charming speech; one should always worship on the eighth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇāṣṭamī*).

Here, after the daily worship (*nityārcanā*), the occasional rite (*naimittika*) is to be performed. Where no restriction regarding time is observed, there the performance of the occasional rites and so forth is to be accepted as extending over either a month or a *maṇḍala*.
And so it is said in the Rudrajāmala: "Whether for half a month, or a month, or twice that, or thrice that—
whenever the attainment of the fruit occurs, one should practice in this manner for that long."
Elsewhere it is also said:
"In the case of rites performed for a specific occasion (naimittika) as well as those for desired ends (kāmya), the attainment of the fruit extends up to the mandala;
provided that one does not perform it with deficient qualities, so that the wise practitioner may partake of the fruit."
Worship of the Goddess on the eighth day bestows the fruit of all desires;
it involves *rambhā* flowers, *bījapūra*, and fragrant substances well-mixed together.
Having mixed [the offerings], one should present the bali, especially on the eighth day;
one should offer a golden garland to Mahādevī, and especially fragrant substances.
One should likewise offer fruit and milk, along with an abundance of sugar;
therefore, with every effort, one should worship Śivā for the sake of prosperity.
One should diligently offer rice grains for the sake of attaining inexhaustible success to the Goddess.
Likewise, in the Nīlatantra:
"And on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, one should worship according to the prescribed rule."
One attains the perfection of command by means of the hibiscus flower and the varvara grass.
One should offer sandalwood paste, flowers, and white aparājitā.
One should especially offer the arghya water at all times during daily worship.
He who diligently worships Durgā on the Mahāṣṭamī day should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times for as many lifetimes as he lives.
He would destroy, at that very moment, the sin accumulated over three lifetimes—
referring to Durgā as "the Savior" (Tāriṇī) because it accords with the context of the section.
O Bhairava, those who worship Mahāmāyā, knowing her according to reality, [attain liberation].
Having attained the perfection of mastery over commands, they certainly go to the abode of Śiva.
Also in the Matsyasūkta:
"Wherever the Tāriṇī exists at a sacred seat (pīṭha) in the form of a stone, one should go there with effort; the measure of the fruit [obtained] is not known."
The mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times where the Tārās reside; with a steady mind and focused attention, accomplishment is attained at that very moment.
He should offer earth prepared with the appropriate number of recitations, as well as unbroken rice grains,
honey, milk-rice, milk with clarified butter, and sugar.
One should offer the *bali* sacrifice, and indeed the offering of a monitor lizard (*godhā*) and liquor (*āsava*) is highly praised.
Also in the *Nīlatantra*: "In this [rite], everything must necessarily be offered, especially by a Brāhmaṇa."
In that case, one should administer jaggery with fresh ginger, or buttermilk mixed with jaggery.
The best of those who know mantras should pour coconut water mixed with honey into a vessel of bronze or copper,
and he should offer the flowers of the plantain tree and the *śala* fish as oblations.
Having attained all accomplishments in succession, one shall finally obtain liberation;
one should offer a thousand oblations of bilva leaves together with unbroken grains of rice.
And on the great eighth day (Mahāṣṭamī), the practitioner obtains charming speech.
Likewise, in the *Mantra-cūḍāmaṇi*:

"On the day of the week belonging to one's own family (*kulavāra*), on the eighth lunar day of one's own family (*kulāṣṭamī*), and especially on the fourteenth day, the worship of the Yoginīs is performed there; therein, the worship of the Kula is paramount."
Just as Viṣṇu, when worshipped on the lunar day sacred to Viṣṇu, bestows all that is desired.
Likewise, when worshipped on a Tuesday coinciding with the lunar day of the Kula, Śakti bestows boons.
Likewise, in the Matsyasūkta:
"One should especially worship on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days;
[offering] water contained in a conch-shell, a full vessel, a hibiscus flower, and barbara grass."
Sandalwood, *arka* flowers, and white *aparājitā*,
as well as especially the gift of food, are prescribed as the constant rule for worship.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times according to the number of days of one's life, or one should recite it a thousand times; listen now to the procedure for the daily worship.
The *kullukā* of Mahogrā is always to be worshipped; it is supreme in worship and always in the performance of hymns, mantras, vows, and so forth.
If one does not perform that [worship], all of it will be fruitless;
yet, he who worships Vāsudeva while maintaining the Great Vidyā—
One attains that fruit correctly and shall obtain union with Hari;
Vāsudeva, Hara, Brahmā, Rāriṇī, and Prakṛti are eternally [one].
She whose single form is always to be meditated upon, she whose single form is eternally established,
the Goddess who bestows heaven and liberation, and who grants the knowledge of victory— therefore,
one should worship that Goddess with perfumes, flowers, and incenses.
One should always worship Tāriṇī with various offerings of food (naivedya) and with devotion.
Now, regarding the special worship on occasional occasions (naimittika), as stated in the Māyātantra:
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the reclining of the deity; in Siṃha, the turning over;
and in Āśvina, one should awaken the Goddess with offerings of meat, milk-rice, and sweetmeats.
O beautiful goddess, awakening at night is better than sleeping during the day;
likewise, even by sleeping during the day, awakening occurs.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, on the Mahāṣṭamī, and on the Ghaṭāṣṭamī— the eighth day of the pitcher [sign]—
the wise person should worship the Lord at night during the months of Māgha and Meṣa.
Now, regarding the worship of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) according to the *Nīlatantra*:
"Among the sacred seats, Kāmarūpa is the supreme seat, yielding great fruit.
O Maheśvara, whatever worship is performed there, even if only once—"
Having abandoned all other seats, I dwell within his body.
Therefore, the Kāmākhyā Yonimaṇḍala is said to possess four times that merit;
O Mahādeva, what more need be said now regarding their fruit?
Where the primordial Tāriṇī dwells together with hosts of crores [of attendants],
that sacred seat (pīṭha) is the mouth of Brahmā, secret and bestowing all happiness.
Since from this the gods, the Vedas, and the sages born of existence all emerge,
therefore always keep it protected.
O Maheśvara, that seat (pīṭha) is indeed twofold: secret and manifest.
The secret one is more meritorious than the manifest, and it is difficult to attain even for the most excellent practitioners.
O Lord of Gods, one obtains [this] everywhere in secret with the beautiful women of the Kula.
Now, regarding the Kula-worship, it is said in the *Tantracuḍāmaṇi*:
"If there is but one who knows the Kula scriptures, O Bhairava, he is worthy of worship therein."
All the gods indeed are worthy of worship—Satya, Brahmā, Śiva, and the others.
O Kulabhairava, if even one young woman there is honored and gazed upon,
all the supreme goddesses are thereby honored.
If one does not especially worship the beloved— who is pure in appearance at the beginning, the end, and the middle— then one will be destroyed by obstacles.
As it is said in the Rudrajāmala:
"To a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, one should give the earth filled with abundant crops."
The fruit that one obtains by giving [those gifts] is obtained from the worship of the Kaula;
even more than from a thousand gifts of food or a hundred sacrifices performed by sacrificers,
that same fruit is attained from providing a meal for the Kaulas.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices, hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices,
and gold equal to Mount Meru [are all equaled by] giving to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
The fruit that one obtains by giving [charity] is obtained from the worship of a *koli* tree;
the fruit that one obtains by performing a sacrifice is obtained from the worship of the Preceptor (*deśika*).
Whatever fruit one obtains from constructing ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, and from making offerings to Śiva and Kṛṣṇa— that same fruit is obtained from the worship of the Guru.
This is the summary.
There is no fruit from what was previously acquired; what need is there to speak of another birth?
Thus says the *Haṃsapārameśvara*.
O Bhairava, the power of man, the power of the animal, and the power of the bird—
when worshipped, they transform meritless action into meritorious action.
If, during the period of *puraścaraṇa*, one should behold a sacred seat (*pīṭha*),
then the worship of that seat is not omitted even if performed only mentally.
One should worship the highly fortunate Bhairavī at Devīkoṭa,
Yoganidrā at Uḍḍīyāna, and Mahiṣāsuramardinī at Kāmarūpa.
[Kātyāyanī] at Kāmabhūti, [Kātyāyanī] named Kāmā at Kāma[dā],
[Pūrṇāśī] at Jālandhara, and Caṇḍikā on Pūrṇaśaila.
Then, O God, the Dikkaravāsinī residing in Kāmarūpa is to be worshipped;
or else, if by good fortune there is a vision of Kāmarūpa itself.
Then, the worship of the goddesses Bhaga and the others is performed there;
on the Kulavāra day, on the Kula-eighth (Kulaṣṭamī), and especially on the fourteenth (Caturdaśī).
In that [rite], the worship of the Yoginīs is the primary thing, as is the worship of the Kula;
just as Viṣṇu, when worshipped on his own lunar day, bestows all desired objects.
Likewise, on an auspicious lunar day (kulatithi), Śakti, the bestower of boons, is worshipped.
Here, the plural form "devīnām" (of the goddesses) beginning with Bhaga is used for the sake of context. As it is stated in the Gāndharva [Tantra]:
"If, by the power of fortune alone, the vision of the Kula arises..."
At that very moment, one should perform a mental worship of them there.
Bhaginī, Bhagājihvā, Bhagāsyā, Bhagamālinī,
Bhagadattā, Bhagākṣī, Bhagakarnā, and Bhagatvacā.

Having worshipped those various women with perfumes and other offerings— those whose noses, breasts, and thighs are marked by the *bhaga* (genital) sign, who move with the grace of the *bhaga*— and having likewise honored the Guru mentally, [one should proceed].
Having performed the salutation according to the prescribed rite, the wise man himself remaining unperturbed,
should worship Viṣṇu on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) according to the Matsyasūkta, and Umāpati on the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī).
On the eighth day, one who desires all supernatural accomplishments should worship Śakti.
Now, the Śivāvali. In the Tantracūḍāmaṇi:
"At the root of a bilva tree, in a wilderness, or even in a cremation ground, the practitioner should offer meat as the primary food-oblation at the time of twilight."
While she was being addressed as "Kālī, Kālī," she, assuming the form of Śiva,
arrived there together with her retinue of attendants who were in the form of bound souls (paśus).
O ornament of the family, when a dog, having eaten, raises its face toward the northeast and barks with a pleasant voice, that alone brings him good fortune; it is not otherwise.
One must certainly and invariably satisfy Śivā with the gift of food,
just as one performs the daily śrāddha, the twilight worship, and the libation to the ancestors.
In the same way, there is a constant duty for those served by the lineage to perform worship of the lineage;
he who does not worship the Goddess Śivā in her form as Paśu in a secluded place [is at fault].
By the howling of a jackal, all of that— his recitation, worship, ritual procedures, and whatever meritorious deeds he has performed— is certainly destroyed instantly.
Having seized and encountered the sinner, Śivā weeps in the desolate wilderness;
O Lord Bhairava, where she, alone with Śiva, must consume him.
Having seen a vulture, one should silently pay homage to Mahākālī;
likewise, having seen a jackal, one should pay homage to Kṣemaṅkarī, the messenger of Yama.
O slender-waisted one, O greatly fierce one, O you with loosened hair, O beloved of Bali,
O you whose face is pleased by the Kulācāra, salutations to you, O beloved of Śaṅkara!
Having seen the hare-marked moon and a corpse, and following them while keeping them to one's right, one should bow down with this mantra;
thus the mantra will yield its fruit.
O you with terrible fangs, O Karālī, who resounds with the cry of a jackal,
who utters deep and dreadful roars— homage to you, O dweller in the cremation ground!
Having beheld her who is the very essence of Tripura, clad in red garments and adorned with red flowers,
one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground and utter this mantra:
O you who resemble the bandhūka flower, O destroyer of fear in the triple city,
O you born from the dawning of good fortune, salutations to you, O lady of excellent complexion!
Likewise, flowers of black color, kings and princes,
elephants, horses, chariots, weapons, shields, and heroic men.
Having seen Mahiṣa (or Mahiṣī), the Lord of the Family, and the Slayer of Mahiṣa,
and having prostrated before her while uttering "Victory to Durgā," one is not touched by obstacles.
O Jayādevī, O Mother of the World, O Primordial Goddess of the Three Cities, O Triple Deity,
O Goddess who grants boons to your devotees, O Slayer of Mahiṣa, I bow down to you.
Upon seeing a vessel of liquor, fish, meat, or a beautiful woman,
and having beheld the goddess Bhairavī and prostrated before her, one should contemplate the mantra.
I bow to you, O boon-granting Goddess adorned with garlands of skulls and bones, for the destruction of terrible obstacles and for the prosperity of the Kula tradition.
I bow to you whose face is completely covered with blood and flesh;
for by the mere sight of these [beings], they would not act otherwise.
If one prioritizes the Śakti-mantra, its accomplishment does not arise.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Determination of Omens, in the *Tārārahasyavṛtti*.
The Fifth Chapter.
Now, the performance of rites for specific desires by those who have mastered the vidyās is written. As for the rites for specific desires, it is stated in the Nīlatantra:
"One who has mastered the mantra should perform the rites for specific desires, and not otherwise."
The characteristics of accomplishment (*siddhalakṣaṇa*) are as stated in the *Svatantratantra*: "The effortless fulfillment of one's desires is declared to be accomplishment (*siddhi*);
[as are] renown, vehicles, ornaments, and the like, as well as the gain [of wealth] and a very long life."
Health, long life, gain, omniscience, and gratitude— these,
O beautiful lady, are said to be the direct accomplishments of one whose mantra has been perfected.
O Dear One, ritual applications (prayoga) should be performed only when the mantra has been mastered, and not otherwise.
As it is stated in the Matsyasūkta:
"The fire-oblation (homa), libation (tarpaṇa), worship (pūjā), meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), and indeed recitation (japa)."
And likewise, the wearing of the yantra for the purposes of killing and suppressing.
These are the optional rites (kāmya-karmāṇi); the procedure for them is different from that of regular worship.
Thus it is stated in the Somabhujagāvalī:
"Śāntika rites are to be known for the winter season, and Pauṣṭika likewise for the late winter;
Ākarṣaṇa in spring, and Vidveṣaṇa in summer."
One should perform the rite of eradication during the rainy season and the rite of killing during the autumn;
the practitioner always performs these rites at these times.
As it is stated in the Rudrajāmala:
"To a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, [one should give] the earth filled with abundant crops."
The fruit that one obtains by giving [those gifts] is obtained from the worship of the Kaula;

the fruit of a thousand gifts of food, and even of hundreds of sacrifices performed by sacrificers, is attained through the gift of food to them [the Kaulas], which results from a meal shared with the Kaula community.
A thousand horse-sacrifices, hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices,
and gold equal to Mount Meru [are not equal to] [giving] to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
The fruit that one obtains by giving [in charity], that fruit is obtained from the worship of a *koli* tree;
the fruit that one obtains by performing a sacrifice, that fruit indeed comes from the worship of a spiritual teacher (*deśika*).
Whatever fruit one obtains from constructing ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, and from making offerings to Śiva and Kṛṣṇa— that same fruit is obtained from the worship of the Guru.
This is the summary.
There is no fruit from what was previously acquired; what need is there to speak of another birth?
Thus says the *Haṃsapārameśvara*.
O Bhairava, since the power of man, the power of the animal, and the power of the bird,
when worshipped, transform meritless action into meritorious action.
If, during the period of *puraścaraṇa*, one should behold a sacred seat (*pīṭha*),
then the worship of that seat is not omitted even if performed only mentally.
One should worship the highly fortunate Bhairavī at Devīkoṭṭa,
Yoganidrā at Uḍḍīyāna, and Mahiṣāsuramardinī at Kāmarūpa.
One should worship Kātyāyanī at Kāmabhūti, Kāmākhyā as the bestower of desires,
Pūrṇaśrī at Jālandhara, and Caṇḍikā on Mount Pūrṇaśaila.
Then, O God, the deity residing in Dikkara should be worshipped in Kāmarūpa;
or else, if by good fortune one beholds Kāmarūpa itself.
Then, worship of the goddesses Bhaga and the others is performed there;
it is especially distinguished on the Kula-day, the Kula-eighth day, and the fourteenth day.
In that [practice], the worship of the Yoginīs is the primary form of Kula worship;
just as Viṣṇu, when worshipped on his own lunar day, bestows all desired objects.
Likewise, on a lunar day (tithi) associated with a [specific] family (kula), Śakrī is worshipped as the bestower of boons.
Here, the plural form "devīnām" (of the goddesses) beginning with Bhagā is used for the sake of the context. As it is said in the Gāndharva [Tantra]:
"If, by the power of destiny alone, the vision of the Kula arises..."
At that very moment, one should perform mental worship (mānasī pūjā) to them there.
Bhaginī, Bhagājihvā, Bhagāsyā, Bhagamālinī,
Bhagadattā, Bhagākṣī, Bhagakarnā, and Bhagatvacā.

Having worshipped those [goddesses]— who possess vulvas, breasts, and private parts, and who move about their private parts— with perfumes and other offerings, as well as mentally, and having likewise worshipped the Guru;
Having paid homage according to the prescribed rite, the wise man himself, remaining unperturbed,
should worship Viṣṇu on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) according to the Matsyasūkta, and Umāpati on the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī).
On the eighth day, one who desires all perfections should worship Śakti.
Now, the Śivāvali. In the Tantracūḍāmaṇi:
"At the root of a bilva tree, or in a wilderness, or even in a cremation ground, the practitioner should offer an oblation consisting primarily of meat at the time of twilight."
When she is to be addressed as "Kālī, Kālī," she there assumes the form of Śiva;
he, in the form of a bound soul (paśu), arrives together with his retinue of attendants.
O ornament of the family, when a dog, having eaten, raises its face toward the northeast and barks with a pleasant sound, that alone brings him auspiciousness; it is not otherwise.
One must certainly and invariably satisfy Śivā with the gift of food,
just as one performs the daily śrāddha, the twilight worship, and the libation to the ancestors.
In the same way, there is constancy in the worship of the lineage regarding those who must be served by the family;
he who does not worship the Goddess Śivā in her form as Paśu in a secluded place [is at fault].
By the howling of a jackal, everything of his— his recitation, worship, ritual procedures, and whatever meritorious deeds he has performed— is certainly destroyed instantly.
Having seized and encountered the sinner, Śivā weeps in the desolate wilderness;
O Lord Bhairava, where it is enjoyed by Śivā alone.
In that very [practice], the supreme delight of all the gods is extremely difficult to attain;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the great worship.
When one has encountered danger from kings and the like, or fears such as those arising from traveling to another country,
one should offer the bali-oblation after reflecting upon one's auspicious and inauspicious karmas.
"Accept it, O Goddess, O highly fortunate Śivā, whose form is like the fire of time!
Reveal the manifestation of the fruits of good and evil; accept this offering for you."
Having recited thus, O beloved of the Kula people, the bali offering should be given.
If the food is not eaten, then it will not be auspicious;
if it is auspicious, then it is eaten there entirely.
Knowing this, O Mahādeva, one should practice that which brings well-being, for there is no other way.
Thus concludes the occasional offering of the *śivāvali*. Now, the rule for the practice of the Śākta tradition is as follows, stated in the *Nīlatantra*:
"Having risen in the morning, the knower of mantras should bow to the *kulavṛkṣa* (the family tree).
Having meditated upon the Guru in the lotus of his own head, he should contemplate it as being bathed by that [Guru's] nectar."
Having propitiated Him with mental offerings, being free from affliction,
one should contemplate the root-mantra from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
One should contemplate one's own body as resembling ten million suns, its form bathed in nectar, and pervaded by a circle of light.

Regarding the determination of the family trees (*kulavṛkṣa*), it is stated in the *Rudrajāmala*: "The *aśoka* tree [is pleased] by a kick of the foot; the *keśara* and *karṇikāra* by the wine from the mouth;
the *cūta* (mango) by a glance; the *tilaka*, *taruṇa*, and *meru* by equality [of treatment]; and the *pīyāla* by song."
The *karṇikāra* tree intoxicates women through conversation, the *kuruvaka* tree through an embrace, the *sindhuvāra* through a glance, and the *campaka* tree surely through touch.
And so it is said in the *Kādambī Mahātantra*: "The *śleṣmātaka*, *karañjaka*, *nimba*, *aśvattha*, *kadambaka*, *bilva*, *vāthā*, and *aśoka*— these are the eight trees of the *kula*."
The Kula-yoginīs abide everywhere within all these [places].
One should not sleep beneath a Kula-tree, nor should one cause any harm there.
And so says the Śruti: "Among the trees of the *kuśa* lineage, there is no sprout [that does not bear fruit].
Whether she be young, intoxicated with youth, old, or beautiful—[in her, one should practice]."
Or, having paid homage to the one who is despised or the great evil one, one should meditate upon her.
One must never, under any circumstances, direct weapons, censure, deceit, or unkindness toward them; otherwise, it will create an obstacle to success.
Women are the gods; women are the vital breaths; women alone are the ornament.
One should always remain attached to women; otherwise, even toward one's own wife, [attachment will fail].
But she will take perverse delight upon his heart;
the flower gathered from her hand, the water gathered from her hand.
One should offer the food gathered by his hand to the deities;
one must avoid other mantras, precedence, and even censure.
This is Brahman; at that time it was that very thing. It is not "I," nor is it even a substantial entity;
it is neither non-existence, nor an effect, nor a cause moving here and there.

In the Kali age, one should avoid these five: expiatory rites, the falling of tears [from the eyes], visiting sacred pilgrimage sites, the offering of funeral cakes as prescribed by the Vedas, and the ritual renunciation of worldly ties.
One should not commit violence against living beings, and especially not violence against animals;
O Goddess, one should avoid all forms of violence except for the offering of a sacrificial oblation (bali).
Now, regarding the conduct of the observance (*samayācāra*): it is said in the *Mantra-cūḍāmaṇi*:
"Listen, O son, to my secret, the defining characteristic of the conduct of the observance;
deprived of which, mantras do not achieve success even in hundreds of aeons."
A man who follows the family scriptures and observes the traditional practices of his lineage becomes a perfected being; there is no doubt that he is devoted to the conduct of a Vaiṣṇava.
One should be patient with the censure of others and always intent on doing good;
whether on a mountain, in a forest, in a secluded place, or in an empty pavilion.
If, by chance, one should find oneself at a crossroads or in the middle of water,
one should meditate for a moment, recite the mantra, and after bowing, proceed as one pleases.
Having seen a vulture, one should pay homage to Mahākālī unobserved;
likewise, having seen a jackal, one should pay homage to Kṣemaṅkarī, the messenger of Yama.
O slender-waisted one, O greatly fierce one, O you who grant boons, O you who are fond of offerings,
O you whose face is pleased by the Kula practice, salutations to you, O beloved of Śaṅkara!
Having seen a hare-marked [moon] or a corpse, and following it while circumambulating to the right,
the practitioner of mantra, having prostrated with this mantra, shall obtain the fruit of the mantra.
O you with terrible fangs and a gaping mouth, who resounds with the cries of jackals and utters deep,
dreadful roars— homage to you, O dweller in the cremation ground!
Having beheld her, who is the very essence of Tripura, wearing red garments and adorned with red flowers,
one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground and recite this mantra:
O you who resemble the bandhūka flower, O destroyer of fear in the three cities,
O you born from the dawning of good fortune, salutations to you, O lady of excellent complexion!
Likewise, flowers of black color, kings and princes,
elephants, horses, chariots, weapons, shields, and heroic men.
Having seen Mahiṣa (or Mahiṣī), the Lord of the Family, and Mahiṣamardinī,
and having prostrated and uttered "Victory to Durgā," one is not touched by obstacles.
O Jayadevī, O Mother of the World, O Primordial One of the Triple City, O Goddess of the Three Deities,
O Goddess who grants boons to your devotees, O Slayer of Mahiṣa, I bow down to you.
Upon seeing a vessel of liquor, fish, meat, or a beautiful woman,
and having beheld the goddess Bhairavī and prostrated before her, one should contemplate the mantra.
I bow to you, O boon-granting Goddess, adorned with garlands of skulls and bones, for the destruction of terrible obstacles and for the prosperity of the family tradition.
I bow to you whose face is completely covered with blood and flesh;
for were it not so, merely by the sight of these [beings], they would surely act in such a way.
If one places the Śakti-mantra at the forefront, its accomplishment does not arise.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Determination of Omens, in the *Tārārahasyavṛtti*.
The Fifth Chapter.
Now, the performance of rites for specific desires (*kāmyānuṣṭhāna*) for those who have mastered the vidyās is written. Regarding the rites for specific desires, it is said in the Nīlatantra:
"One who has mastered the mantra should perform the rites for specific desires; not otherwise."
The characteristics of accomplishment (*siddhalakṣaṇa*) are as stated in the *Svatantratantra*: "The effortless fulfillment of one's desires is declared to be accomplishment (*siddhi*);
likewise, renown, the acquisition of vehicles, ornaments, and the like, and a very long life."
O beautiful lady, for one whose mantra is perfected, health, long life, gain, omniscience, gratitude, and the direct accomplishment of all powers are said to be attained.
O Dear One, the ritual applications (prayoga) must be performed when the mantra has been mastered, and not otherwise.
As it is stated in the Matsyasūkta:
"The fire-oblation (homa), the libation (tarpaṇa), the worship (pūjā), the meditative visualization (bhāvanā), and indeed the recitation (japa)."
Likewise, the wielding of the yantra, as well as its slaying and suppression.
These are the optional rites (*kāmyakarma*); their performance is different from the regular worship (*samarcana*).
Thus it has been stated in the Somabhujagāvalī:
"Peaceful rites are to be known as appropriate in the cool season (śiśira), and likewise nourishing rites in the late winter (hemanta);
attraction in the spring, and likewise incantations for causing dissension in the summer."
One should perform expulsion during the rainy season and killing during the autumn;
the practitioner always performs these [rites] at these times.
Midnight is the autumn season, and the forenoon is the winter;
the afternoon shall be spring, and midday is indeed the summer.
The afternoon is known as the form of the rainy season, and the evening twilight is remembered as the cold season.
In the *Kṛtyāpallava*,
it is said that the application of *ūṣā* occurs at dawn during the winter, at the onset of the cool season (*śiśira*),
at half a watch (*praharārdha*) during spring, and on the final day of the month during summer.
And during the fourth watch known as *varṣā*, when the sun has set in autumn—this is an elliptical expression for the six rites (*ṣaṭkarma*). As it is stated in the *Bhairavasrotas*:
"Pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*)—these four."
The six rites have been employed, as well as suppression and death.
Now, their characteristics,
the removal of diseases, malevolent rites, planetary influences, and so forth, as well as the performance of pacification (śānti),
prosperity (puṣṭi), and the attainment of wealth, people, knowledge, and other such things, shall be described.
The deluding of people, subjugation, attraction, and bringing [others] under one's own control,
as well as the performance of rites such as expulsion and so forth, is proclaimed as *nigraha* (suppression).
The taking of people's life-breaths is proclaimed as "killing" (māraṇa).
Now, regarding the temporal regulation for these [rites], it is stated in the *Kṛtyāpallava*:
"Beginning from sunrise, for ten *ghaṭikās* day after day."
The seasons, beginning with the summer solstice, [constitute] day and night, day after day.
Spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the cool season—
winter is known for rites of pacification, summer is declared for inciting enmity, the rainy season is known for causing upheaval, and autumn for the act of killing.
One should visualize [the deity] as red in color for subjugation, attraction, and immobilization;
as white for neutralizing poison, pacification, nourishment, and expansion;
as yellow for the rite of immobilization; and one should remember it as smoky-grey for causing agitation.
In the rite of driving away madness, one should visualize [the deity] resembling Śatru-gopa; and in the rite of killing, he should be black in color.
One should meditate on [the victim] as standing when performing a rite of killing; it is taught that one should meditate on him as sleeping when performing a rite of expulsion.
O Goddess of the Suras, one should visualize [the deity] as seated for rites such as subjugation (vaśya);
and for rites of pacification (śāntika), one should visualize him as seated and white in color.
That which stands on the path of the Left (Vāmamārga) is proclaimed as black and characterized by tamas;
that of sattva is for those desiring liberation, and that of rajas is for those desiring sovereignty.
The *tāmasa* [mantra] is employed for the destruction of enemies, the warding off of all diseases,
for killing, the neutralization of poisons, the expulsion of malevolent planets and spirits,
and for eradication and inciting enmity; it is applied using five colors.
The name preceded by the mantra is proclaimed as being at the side;
the placement of the name at the end of the mantra is designated as "yoga."
In rites for pacification, nourishment, subjugation, expiation and purification,
as well as for delusion and illumination, the wise employ this yoga.
He is said to be employed in the rites of immobilization (stambhana), eradication (uccāṭana), destruction (uccheda), and sowing dissension (vidveṣa).
When the mantra is placed at the beginning, end, and middle of the name, it is called "yoga."
It is said to be for bringing about the presence of the mantra, for warding off all sins,
and for the pacification of fever, planetary influences, poison, and magical spells.
In the *sammelana* [method], those very same meanings and syllables of the mantras are joined such that each is separated by one; that is proclaimed as *grathana*.
When the mantra is placed at the beginning and end of the name for the purpose of pacification, that constitutes a "sandwiched" (sampuṭa) form; this is defined as the "stake" (kīlaka).
The "pillar" (*stambha*) is prescribed for the *mṛtyuñjaya* [mantra], while the "encasement" (*saṃpuṭa*) is used for protection and other purposes;
two mantra-syllables are placed on both sides, with the syllables of the name in between them in sequence.
That [mantra] is to be strung together for the purposes of subjugation, attraction, and nourishment.
Thus has the sequence of yoga been declared by the wise for the time of ritual action;
one should recite "svāhā" during the fire-rite and "namaḥ" everywhere in worship.
For pacification, nourishment, subjugation, hatred, eradication, and killing,
one should employ, in sequence, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, *vaṣṭ* (*vaṣaṭ*), *hūc* (*hūm*), *voṣaṭ*, and the syllable *phaṭ*.
For rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), one should use the lotus posture (padmāsana); for pacification (śāntika), the auspicious posture (svastikāsana);
for attraction (ākṛṣṭi), the heel-lock posture (pārṣṇika); and likewise for inciting enmity (vidveṣa) and the subjugation of enemies.
The *sarvasvastika* is praised for expulsion (*uccāṭana*) and killing (*māraṇa*) and so forth;
however, for pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), and subjugation (*vaśya*), the *sundarī* with its beautiful intention is excellent.
Blazing with all her ornaments, her mind’s distress fully appeased,
the goddess should be worshipped properly, her lotus-face perfectly serene.
It is likewise praised for summoning and for slaying. The subject to be acted upon may be one who is summoned, or one who is hated, or one who is being oppressed even by his own people,
or one who is being tormented by the people with punishments, or one who has been seized by Takṣaka.
When possessed by an owl or a crow, or when seized for the purpose of eradication,
the enemy should recite [the mantra] while mounted upon a corpse, biting his lips in anger.
The mantra-practitioner should perform the rites according to the proper rule,
whether they be cruel deeds or rites for prosperity and so forth, in accordance with the specific lunar day, constellation, and conjunction.
These should be employed according to the prescribed rule, which is now being fully declared:
namely, the fifth, the second, the third, and likewise the seventh.
The ninth lunar day (navamī) joined with the day of Mercury or Jupiter is honored for rites of pacification (śānti);
it is likewise recommended for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), as are the eighth (aṣṭamī) and seventh (saptamī).
The tenth and eleventh lunar days joined with Sunday, Friday, and so forth;
likewise, the new moon day, the ninth, and the first for the purpose of attraction (ākarṣaṇa).
The full moon day conjoined with Saturn is for the rite of causing enmity;
likewise, the fourteenth and eighth days of the dark fortnight when the stars are dim are the recommended lunar days for the rite of eradication,
especially at the time of dusk.
The fourteenth day, the eighth day, and likewise the new moon day of the dark fortnight.
The fifth and tenth lunar days, when conjoined with a Saturday or a Tuesday, are auspicious for rites of killing; likewise, they are auspicious when conjoined with a Wednesday or a Monday.

The full moon day should be known as the lunar date for the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*). One should perform auspicious rites during the rising of auspicious planets and at a favorable moment.
Killing is performed during fierce rites, on a day when the sun is in its waning phase, and during the Mṛtyu-yoga.
Regarding libation, it is declared in the Matsyasūkta that libation with honey fulfills all desires.
It directly brings about the accomplishment of mantras and destroys even the great sins.
In the Nīlatantra it is also said:
"One should indeed offer libations for a month with water mixed with camphor;
having brought all kings under one's control, one shall enjoy pleasures for as long as one lives."
With clarified butter filled [in the vessel], one’s fame is perfected; with milk, for the sake of freedom from disease; and with incense sticks mixed with agallochum, one shall be happy at all times.
With waters mixed with coconut water, for the accomplishment of all goals.
One should destroy enemies by using [the powder] mixed with black pepper and hot water.
One may cause enemies to vanish in an instant by means of hot water alone;
one afflicted by fever shall be restored to health by sprinkling with milk.
The method of recitation is precisely as follows. It is stated in the *Nīlatantra*:
"Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) with hair unbound, one should recite ten thousand [mantras] with devotion;
his speech, whether in prose or verse, shall become entirely effective."
In that very state, through meditation, the Piṅgākṣī causes [the target] to be eradicated; the Kekarā terrifies;
the Muktāsyā puts to flight; and the Ghurṇitā causes [the target] to tremble with fear.
When agitated, she causes disturbance; when well-disposed, she brings about accomplishment;
when obstructed, she causes contraction; and when deceived, she awakens one to reality.
In the *Phetkārīya* as well, here everything must be performed through meditation (*bhāvanā*) and the contemplation of mantras.
In rites such as eradication (*uccāṭana*) and the like, the recitation (*japa*) is always [to be done] everywhere in conjunction with the *ayuta* [number]. As it is said in the *Siddhasārasvata*:
By merely reciting [the mantra] one hundred times,
a wise practitioner who applies a mark of *rocanā* (cow bezoar) will cause anyone whom he looks upon to become like a servant.
In the *Phetkārīya* [Tantra] as well, it is said:
"In a deep lotus pond, a staff or a piece of wood [is used]; in a house in the dark..."
Having quickly brought it with one's teeth, one should fashion a peg from it.
With that very [substance] mixed with honey and ghee, one should write the root mantra interlaced [with the name] in the middle of a series of lines upon a lotus leaf.
Having cast those [flowers] into a square sacrificial pit,
one should also offer a thousand oblations of red lotuses soaked in milk and water.

The meaning of this is as follows: "In a house of darkness" means when the moon or the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu. "Having cast [it]" means one should cast it into the middle of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) at a depth of twelve finger-breadths. "Interwoven with the root mantra" means that within the *hṛllekhā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) and the letter *ra* of the root mantra, one inserts: *mama drutakavitvasiddhiṃ kuru kuru*.

One should write [the mantra] together with this designation. Then follows another ritual application: one should offer an oblation (*bali*) at a crossroads with the Padmāvatī mantra. With the mantra "Oṃ padmaṃ padme mahāpadme padmāvati māye svāhā," one should offer the oblation as previously described in the chapter on occasional rites (*naimittika-paṭala*). This is stated in the *Phetkārīya*:
Having first uttered the syllable *praṇava*, one should likewise utter the pair of words "Padme," then say the word "Mahāpadme," and thereafter the word "Padmāvati."
One should offer the bali-oblation with the mantra "māye svāhā" as before;
the man who performs the rite in this manner shall become a swift poet.

Then, for the sake of accomplishing everything, one should offer the bali at a crossroads at night, either with the bali-mantra to be described hereafter or with the bali-mantra prescribed for the daily worship (nityapūjā). As it is stated in the Phetkārīya:
"By means of this specific ritual service (upacāra), one may bring a queen under one's control."
By the mere recitation [of this mantra], the entire world was subdued by Bali, as if by a king.

The meaning of this is "by means of a specific ritual offering. As it is stated in the *Matsyasūkta*: "Having mixed together the *rambhā* fruit, the *jātī* flower, and fragrant citron, one should present the offering, especially on the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*)."

"By mere recitation alone" means by means of [recitation] devoid of worship and so forth. "The king becomes submissive through the application of yoga and the like" refers to the minor branches [of practice].

"The entire world [is subdued] by the *bali* offering" is to be understood by connecting it with the chapter on occasional rites (*naimittika-paṭala*) as stated in the *Matsyasūkta*. This is also stated in the *Nīlatantra*:
If one would accomplish this through the ritual application, this is the *bali*-mantra for the application;
then, at midnight, one should always offer the *bali* at a crossroads.
It wards off enemy armies, planetary portents, misfortunes, diseases, and magical spells;
having first uttered the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should then utter "Ugratāre."
One should utter the two syllables "Vikaṭadaṃṣṭre" while deluding the opposing faction;
then one should state the pair "Māraya Khādaya" and likewise the pair "Paca [Tathā]."

"Those who are intent on harming me with circles of yoginīs—consume them! HŪM PHAṬ SVĀHĀ! Attract the supreme vidyā! Cut it! Seize it in the skull-cup! SVĀHĀ! With this mantra, which is also a bali-mantra, one should then offer the bali-oblation according to one's preference.

In this context, the offering of the sacrificial animal (bali) such as a goat follows as a secondary point, as stated in the *Kālitantra*: "Having placed an animal with auspicious marks before the Goddess, having sprinkled it with water consecrated by the [Name-mantra], having protected it with the Astra-mantra, having veiled it with the Kavaca-mantra,
having rendered it nectar with the Dhenu-mudrā, and holding it by the ear, one recites this mantra:"

One should recite: "We meditate upon the Lord of Beings (Paśupati), we contemplate Viśvakarman; may Jīva inspire us. Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should worship the sword [with]: "Drīṃ! Kāli Kāli Vajreśvarīlo daṇaḍāyai namaḥ.
Then, one should worship [with]: "Hūṃ! To Vāgeśvarī Brahmāṇyā, namaḥ. Hūṃ!"
Salutations to Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. Hūṃ! Salutations to Umā and Maheśvara.

With this mantra, and saying "Salutations to the sword spoken by the powers of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva," one should take hold of it and worship it, [reciting]: "O Sword, you who destroy the enemy's voice, intent upon the accomplishment of the task of power!"

"O Lord of the Sword, salutations to you! If this is an animal, [release it] quickly. Then, taking *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and water with the root mantra, one who desires victory—characterized by long life, the cessation of famine and suffering, the attainment of the supreme state, and eternal, uninterrupted joy—[should perform the rite].

"O illustrious Nīlasarasvatī, I offer this animal to you. Having requested the command of the Goddess, he should present the animal according to the prescribed ritual: "May it be offered to you according to the stated injunction. Then, if it falls on the right side, it is auspicious; if on the left side, it is censured.
O Goddess, the wise one should remember that when it falls in the middle, it is the state of wretchedness (dainya) and a fracture (chedda).
Then, having gone near the sacrificial pit, with fifteen oblations,
he should offer a well-characterized *bali* while producing that very same fault.

Then, one should offer the *bali*—consisting of blood, meat, and cooked rice—with the mantras of the *baṭukas*, *yoginīs*, *kṣetrapālas*, Gaṇeśa, and others. In the southeast (āgneyī), having worshipped with perfumes, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and flowers while reciting: *Hūṃ Vāṃ, obeisance to Vaṭuka Bhairava*; and in the northwest (vāyavyā), [having worshipped] with perfumes and unbroken rice while reciting: *Hūṃ Yāṃ, obeisance to the Yoginīs*.

Having worshipped with flowers in the northeast (īśāna) with "Hūṃ Kṣāṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla," and having worshipped with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers in the southwest (nairṛta) with "Hūṃ Gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa," one should offer the bali-oblation.
Taking charcoal from a cremation ground on a Tuesday night,
one should wrap it in a black cloth and bind it with a red thread;
having consecrated it one hundred times with mantras, one should cast it into the house of the enemy.
Within seven days, this great rite of eradication shall take effect upon them.
Thus it is said in the Phetkārīya:
"One should write the mantra upon human bone with turmeric mixed with alkali; having recited it one thousand times at night on a Saturday."
If it falls upon one's house, death will occur for that person within three months;
if upon a field, there will be loss of crops; if upon a horse, there will be loss of speed.

The loss of wealth occurs in the house of wealth, while its total depletion occurs in the middle of the village. *Kṣāra* consists of six salts combined with *śyena-viṭ*. In the *hṛllekhā* mantra, between the lower *ta* and the middle *repha*, one inserts:
"O [Name] and [Name], create hatred, create hatred! This has been stated in the *Nīlatantra*:
For the rite of hatred, however, the wise one should inscribe the mantra upon a cloth from a corpse;
having written the names of both the object of hatred and the hater, that hater shall become greatly afflicted by hatred.

"One should write the mantra" means that having written the mantra, one should include the name of the target (sādhya) such as "Kill so-and-so, kill so-and-so" in the middle of the *repha* of the *hṛllekhā*. Alternatively, having written the name of the target, one should write the mantra at its end.

"Having recited it a thousand times" refers to the recitation of the mantra at the end of "Kill so-and-so, kill so-and-so. However, in the case of inciting hatred (*dveṣa*), [the procedure is as follows]:...
At the end of the mantra "Kuru kuru dveṣam amukāmukayoḥ," one should recite the mantra a thousand times. Now, he states another yoga: as it is said in the *Saṅketatantra*:
The word "uccāṭaya" (expel) is proclaimed, followed by "piṅgākṣa";
then, having uttered the mantra "ṣaṭ hūṃ," one should place the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) before it.
The enemy moves from one place to another like a second crow;
"Piṅgākṣa" is the seed-syllable *phrem*, because it was spoken by Bhūtabhairava. "Piṅgākṣa" means "crooked-eyed. Now, he describes the destruction of the power of the supreme mantra:
Having written the enemy’s vidyā upon a leaf of the *kumuda* lotus within a fire-enclosure (*vahnipuṭa*),
one should recite the mantra in a cremation ground, enclose it, and then perform the *vidarbha* (interlacing) ritual.
Even if recited for a thousand lifetimes, this vidyā does not bestow its fruit;
even the siddhis that are difficult for the gods to attain will perish.
The remedy for that is as follows:
one should write the syllable *amṛta* within the circle of the Mothers (*mātṛcakra*), moisten it with nectar (*amṛta*), and cast it into water while reciting the mantra: "May they purify us."
Whatever mantra he recites is instantly consumed like the rising moon;
yet, though he has become an object of hatred for the brahmins, he remains radiant moment by moment.
Now, the yantra for wearing [as an amulet] for rites such as pacification (śāntika) is described:
the practitioner of mantra should write the mantra with a golden stylus within a pair of yonis;
thereafter, he should inscribe the long vowels, excluding the neuter ones, within the hexagon.
The best of practitioners should draw an eight-faced [diagram] within the bhūpura.
O lady of excellent vows, one should write this on a golden plate, or on birch bark, or even on silver, using a golden stylus and accompanied by the eight fragrant substances.
"Or else, having drawn [the figure] with a stalk of dūrvā grass or again with daśamūla," thus it is said.
In the *Ekavīrākalpa*,
it states that once it has been wrapped in a yellow cloth, one should enclose it with lac.
One should tie it with a silk thread as an ornament for the necks of children.
For women, it is on the left arm, and for others, on the right arm.
A barren woman obtains a son, and one who is poor becomes wealthy.
This protection was established of old by Gītama and others for the sake of knowledge;
it was also proclaimed by Pāthira and others who desired victory in battle.

The meaning of this is as follows: within a six-cornered [diagram] formed by two joined triangles (yoniyugma), one should prepare ink using saffron, gorocana, and sandalwood on birch bark or similar material using a golden stylus. Having written the root mantra in sequential lines, one should place the syllable *hṛllekhā* (hrīṃ) in the middle of the letter *ra*, followed by: "protect, protect [the name] so-and-so" (*amukasya rakṣāṃ kuru kuru*) and "of [the names] such-and-such women" (*amukīnām*).

Having written "O auspicious one, procreate a son" (*śubha putram utpādaya*) and "accomplish the attainment of knowledge for me" (*asya jñānasiddhiṃ kuru kuru*), etc., together with the objective (*sādhya*), one should write the letters excluding the neuter vowels—namely those devoid of *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*—within the hexagon; for it is said:
"Among the vowels, that group of four which stands in the middle is the neuter."
One should write the long vowels—ā, ī, ū, ai, au, and aḥ—one by one. On the eight petals, the eight syllables are as follows:
ai / drā / a / ai / drī / phaṭ / svāhā. As it has been said:
"The Vāgbhava [syllable], the Kula goddess, the Tāraka, and likewise the Vāgbhava."
The mantra for Hṛllekhā consists of the weapon-mantra at the end, concluding with the wife of fire (svāhā).
The eight-syllable mantra has been proclaimed; it is said to be the essence of all mantras.
Other ritual applications (prayogas) taught for Kālikā-vidyā should also be performed here. As it is stated in the Phetkārīya:
"One should perform here the ritual applications taught in the Kālikā-mantra-tantra."

Regarding this, it has been correctly stated that one should also perform the ritual applications therein; now, as for the consecration of the child: before the cutting of the umbilical cord, one should wipe the tongue three times with the right hand using honey and parched grain, and then with a golden probe and white *dūrvā* grass.

One should write [the mantra] on the tip of a sacrificial wood splinter, or on the tongue or the lip of the child. This writing is a purificatory rite (saṃskāra) performed immediately after the birth of a son; having formed a row [of letters], one should write it. Some say it should be done on the eleventh day; for Kṣatriyas, on the fifteenth day, and for Vaiśyas...

"For Śūdras, it is on the twenty-fifth day, or at the end of the month. Regarding this, the gurus say that one should first worship the deity and then write the mantra. However, in the *Mahogratārākalpa*, one should worship the deity afterwards. If the father is away, then the maternal uncle or the paternal uncle should write it. This has been stated in the *Matsyasūkta*:
Alternatively, before the umbilical cord is cut, one should write [the mantra] with a golden stylus upon the tongue of the child using honey and parched grain.
The practitioner of mantras should write the root mantra on the lip with white *dūrvā* grass;
by merely uttering it once, one becomes eloquent and a swift poet.
In that very context,
the rite of birth-consecration (*janmasaṃskāra*) is praised when a son is born;
one should write the mantra upon the tongue with a splinter of sacrificial wood.
Having swept three times with the right hand alone,
one should recite the mantra for each individual row and make it beautifully orderly.
First, the consecration (saṃskāra) must be performed; at its conclusion, one should write the mantra. Then, with perfumes, sandalwood, and flowers, one should worship Śivā at the end of that.
Facing north, one should place the supreme pedestal;
one should worship the goddess Tāriṇī with various beautiful offerings of food. Thus, the son shall become a poet, eloquent, truthful, and one who has conquered his senses.
The elder brother should write the mantra, and likewise the mother’s brother;
the father himself should also write the mantra, and never anyone else at all.
Having carefully placed the child on his mother's lap and covered it with a cloth,
he, being self-restrained, should perform a rite for the child's peace together with Brāhmaṇas.

Just as one desires this son among those born of desire, [wishing] "May he remain right here," so for Tārā— [who] nourishes all these virtuous beings from the gods with auspicious peace— for Keśava, for Tārā, for the Rudras, for Śiva, and for the glory of Śiva. At the conclusion of writing the mantra, one should perform a rite of peace with a benediction (*svastyayana*).
Then one should recite the Śāntistotra into the ear of his mother;
likewise, one should perform the recitation of the hymn into their left ears:
"O Mother, O Goddess, salutations to you, O sinless one who bears the form of Brahman."
O Kṛṣā, remove my obstacles; grant me the perfection of mantra.
O Māheśī, O goddess who bestows boons, you whose form is supreme bliss!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the accomplishment of the mantra!
O Kaumārī, sovereign of all vidyās, you who are excellent in sporting with Kumāra!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra,
O Goddess who bears the form of Viṣṇu and who carries the son of Vinatā.
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the accomplishment of the mantra,
O Goddess who assumes the form of an enemy and is worshipped by the gods beginning with Śakra!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the accomplishment of the mantra;
O Cāmuṇḍā, you who are smeared with blood from garlands of severed heads, you who destroy all impediments!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of mantra;
O Mahālakṣmī, you of great energy, who destroy agitation and terror!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of mantra;
O Goddess who consists of the Mothers, O Mother who dwells beyond the Mothers!
O Goddess, you who are manifold and of universal form, salutations be to you!
Whoever, being self-restrained, recites this hymn at the commencement of undertakings,
or upon seeing a clever woman, no obstacles shall arise for him.
O son, these have been described to you as the door-deities of one of noble lineage;
however, if they are not worshipped at the time of initiation or during the occasion of daily worship, [the result is lost].
"O child, the fruit of his worship is carried away by Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.

Thus ends the *Śāntistotra*. Thus ends the fifth chapter (*paṭala*), the determination of the performance of optional rites (*kāmyānuṣṭhāna-nirṇaya*), in the *Tārārahasya*. This was written by Śaṅkara, the grandson of Lambodara and son of Kamalākara.
The Determination of the Performance of Optional Rites.
Now begins the sixth chapter.

Now, all the accomplishments (*siddhi*) dependent upon the meditation on the Mahācīnakrama have been set forth in this tantra. To explain how that is so: it is stated in the *Tārāṇava*: The Goddess said:
"O Lord, the Mahācīnakrama has been described; it is difficult to find on earth."
Likewise, the Gāndharva and Cīna scripts, and whatever else is most secret and great.
O Lord, the Mahācīnakrama has been indicated but not fully revealed;
tell it now, if you have affection for me.
The Blessed One said:
"O Goddess, the Mahācīnakrama is hidden within all tantras; it must not be spoken of in the three worlds, O noble lady, except with a state of pure devotion."
Some were gods, some humans, some Dānavas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas;
there were those from the world of the Nāgas, Kinnaras, and hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Whatever herds of animals, whatever wings, and whatever beings exist within the world—
all these are utterly insentient and by nature mutually antagonistic.
All are devoted to false imaginings and are eager for the vision of wrong paths.
Among these, O Great Goddess, no one knows that Brahman which is consciousness, bliss, and the joy of awareness; how then can I explain it to you?

O Goddess of lovely limbs, O sinless one, that which has been spoken here for your sake concerns the nature of one who is eternally liberated; please forgive me, and you need not say anything further.
The Goddess said:
Salutations to you who are the form of Śiva; salutations to you who are the form of the Guru. Salutations to you, O Lord, the giver of boons; salutations to the treasure-house of compassion.
For those who do not delight in other gods and those who long for your feet— for my devotees alone is the superior fruit established.
Lions, tigers, and the like, as well as those who act as obstacles,
all enemies, and whatever other malevolent creatures there may be;
They go to destruction in that [fire] like moths in a flame;
the body, appearing like the crest of a lamp, is seen by wicked beings.
O Lord, O Sovereign, have the five deities become identical with Śiva on their seats through your own power alone, or rather, through the state of pure love?
Earth turns into water, and water becomes composed of fire;
fire likewise [dissolves] into air, and air [dissolves] into space, which is its illuminator.
All the Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and whatever other hosts of deities there may be,
as well as the kings— all these follow your path in the blinding darkness.
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and the servants of Yama obey his command;
wherever there may be a desire, that very thing is placed within the hand of accomplishment.
The goddess Gopini always attends upon him with unwavering speech out of fear.
Having abandoned the state of duality, what else remains to be spoken at length?
One who seeks liberation attains liberation; one who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth.
And in the end, he is born in the world of Gaurī like a second Śiva.
May my devotees attain success; speak before me.
This must not be told to one who is not a devotee, nor to one devoted to another, nor to a sinner.
The Blessed One said:
"O Goddess, the Mahācīnakrama has been described on earth as being of three kinds."
As it is said in the Vīra-tantra:
"Bathing and so forth are mental purification; the recitation of the *praṇava* is mental."
Mental worship is divine; mental visualization and so forth are all auspicious. No time whatsoever is inauspicious;
there is no distinction between day and night, nor between the twilights and the dead of night.

One should not practice purification here through the mind by means of clothing and the like, nor through the body by means of water and so forth; rather, one should practice with a mind free from conceptual construction.
In this [practice], there is no requirement for purification, nor is there any defect such as impurity;
the mantra-practitioner who contemplates thus attains the fulfillment of all desires.
His speech, consisting of both prose and verse, arises in the assembly;
by the mere sight of him, the disputants are considered shorn of their luster.
For even kings resort to servitude; what then of other people?
One should always worship the Goddess, even if one has not bathed or has already eaten.
At midnight, in a pure place, one should cause the offering to be given with the bali-mantra.
One must never harbor hatred toward women; indeed, the worship of women is especially important.
Having placed a large conch shell at the place of recitation, one should perform the recitation while facing upward;
even while approaching, touching, or looking at a woman, or wherever else one may be, provided one has not yet undergone the tonsure ceremony.
He offered betel, other foods, and various edible substances according to his taste,
as well as fish, meat, curd, honey, and other such edibles according to his preference.
Having consumed foods of every possible form, one should perform the recitation of the mantra while eating;
herein there is no restriction regarding direction or time, nor any rule concerning posture and the like.
In the practice of this great mantra, there is no fixed rule for the time of recitation, nor for worship and the like, nor even for the offerings; here, it is said that one may follow one's own will.
If it is entwined by creepers numbering as many as the lunar days (tithis),
then success shall be attained within a month by performing one thousand recitations.
If it is recited twice as much on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days,
then at that very moment there is great accomplishment, difficult even for the gods to attain.
Having written the seed-syllable with saffron upon a great Chinese tree,
and having inscribed the name of the person to be acted upon beside it, one should strike it with glances and showers [of mantras].
Afflicted by desire, she goes to wherever she may find him.
