Having prepared a bolus smeared with the juice of the great *cīna* tree,
O Goddess, he whose name it is offered shall meet his death before long.
With the piths of the great Chinese tree and its creepers, and with bilva leaves.
Having worshipped the Goddess a thousand times in the cremation ground, the most excellent practitioner—
Then one attains the kingdom, provided one does not flee;
for this kingdom has women as its root, and such a lineage is beautiful everywhere.
Even the gods are not worth a sixteenth part of that;
the entry into the house of the creeper yields a fruit far greater than the corpse-seat.
O Goddess, such a practitioner is always difficult to find on earth. Whoever is seen anywhere on earth, by whatever means or in whatever form, O Goddess,
death occurs from the disclosure of this [secret], and not otherwise.
Whether it be this disparagement of the practitioner or of this mantra,
I shall take away everything from him, together with the hosts of great spirits.

Together with the circle of Yoginīs, she herself effects their destruction. Now follows the application for Sarasvatī: as it is stated in the *Phetkārīya*, "By merely placing [the mantra] upon the tongue, even a mute becomes a skilled poet."
This is its meaning: some say that one should place the hand on the mouth with the thought that it is the *vidyā* upon the tongue and then recite;
others say it is the marking of the tongue at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the purification of the child. But in reality, [it is] in the form of radiant energy (*tejas*).
"One should meditate on the Vidyā upon the tongue"—this is the meaning of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). (This is the secret meaning. As it is said in the *Vīratantra*:
"He who meditates upon Tāriṇī in the form of a lamp upon his tongue..."
The poetry of one who stands equal to Bṛhaspati has surpassed (or composed) that of Śukra.
In the *Nīlatantra* it is also said:
"Having risen during the *brāhma* muhūrta and performed the necessary duties, the wise man, being well-restrained,
should meditate on the Vidyā in the form of light upon his tongue and recite it."
His speech becomes nectar-showering in every way.
According to the Ekavīrā-kalpa:
"In the morning, having visualized the Vidyā in the form of a lamp upon the tip of the tongue..."
One should drink water while reciting the Vidyā together with the Mātṛkā once.
By means of the prescribed method of drinking water, even one who is mute may become a skilled poet; through the constant practice of contemplation, the practitioner becomes virtuous,
wise, a poet, eloquent, a great yogi, and a partaker of liberation— of this there is no doubt.
In this regard, the procedure is as follows: taking a water-pot in the right hand, one should recite the *mātṛkā* while sprinkling water.

Herein lies the secret of the recitation: having pronounced the vowels together with their nasal bindus (*sabindu*), and then having pronounced them without the nasal bindus (*nirbindu*), one should arrest the breath of utterance, cause it to reach the supreme bindu (*parabindu*), and remain there for a single moment in the form of abiding.

One should recite [the mantra]. Then, having recited in that manner by means of the yoga of exhalation (*recaka*), one should bring the water held in the hollow of the hand. Thereafter, one should drink that water; this is the secret meaning. This yoga should be practiced for the duration of a year. According to the *Svatantratantra*, after one year, his fourfold proficiency arises.
Now, another secret [is taught]. It is stated in the Vīratantra:

"Having inscribed the letters of the mantra upon the excellent womb of a Kula-youthful woman, one [should likewise inscribe] all the mantras of the Vedas that are afflicted by sleep, defects, and so forth."
Having mastered the external and internal phonemes of the Guru’s school according to the prescribed rules,
one who is pure-minded should accomplish [the goal] by reciting them with focused attention.
O Mother, may that person who, following the noble path, establishes you upon their own ground with the waters of sacred fords— be they immeasurable— [attain success].
One who, with the thought of Him, meditates upon Him whose fragrant form is fashioned with red and fresh flowers, perfumes, garlands, and unguents.
He who, having performed worship with the well-known retinue of yoginīs preceded by the nyāsas,
serves her who is born of a perfectly pure lineage and is free from shame and aversion.
He himself has conquered his limbs, yet he causes agitation among the yoginīs; touching the *kulacakra* of the Enemy of Paśu (Śiva), he is a tree of heroes with branches in the center—
a mortal fallen by a curse who has become the Lord of the Gods.
Having joined the two— the Kulapathi and the Kulanatha— one should join that which is outside them, having reflected upon it as encapsulated by Manu.

O Mother, may he who is skilled in the arts, whose mind is free from evil intent, and who is like the moon— having dispelled the net of darkness consisting of fear and despondency— depict you in three ways as the expert in all arts.
With his body covered by the masses of pollen streaming from the creepers of the feet of those worthy of divine worship,
that wise one serves him who is the Lord worthy of worship for liberation.
Now follows the great secret conducive to the accomplishment of mantras. In the *Viśuddheśvara Mahātantra*, the Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, be gracious, O Lord of Gods, who are devoted to the welfare of all living beings!"
O Śaṅkara, tell me the means by which success will certainly be attained.
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme knowledge, the most excellent among all knowledges,
by the mere realization of which the Vidyā quickly becomes propitious.

The power within the root tuber, which has the form of a serpent, is this very thing called the *prāṇa* by the wise; it consists of the wind of the *ārtava* (menstrual/seasonal) blood and the *abhram* (cloud/vapor).
The jhillikās, constantly rising, warble with an indistinct sweetness;
they depart through the aperture of Brahma and enter the beautiful abode.
One should effect the dissolution of the mind there by means of the very sequence of going and coming;
by that, the instruction in mantra is born, which is the lamp bestowing all accomplishments.
Just as nothing at all appears to us in a house filled with darkness,
so too mantras devoid of the *śikhā* never attain accomplishment.
O Supreme Goddess, the instruction on the crest-lock (śikhā) is concealed everywhere;
without this [instruction], there shall be no accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of years.
Therefore, O Girijā, you too must guard this with great effort.
Now, another secret from the Nīlatantra:
"Suptā (asleep), nidrāyitā (dozing), mattā (intoxicated), vidrāvaṇaratā (delighting in causing flight), and parā (the supreme)."
Kulasundarī is bound by the entire web of defects.
The night-walker, the day-walker, the twilight-walker, and the sprout;
the piercing with Darbha grass, the conjunction of seeds, and likewise the conjunction of states of being.
Having understood this, the Guru should awaken the seed-syllable; he alone is the cause in this matter.

"Night-wandering" (*niśicāra*) and so forth: "night-wandering" is the arising of the breath in the left nostril; likewise, the arising of the breath in the right nostril is "day-wandering" (*divāvāra*); "junction-wandering" (*sandhācāra*) is both channels.
The continuous flow [of the breath]. As it is stated in the *Viṣṇusaṃhitā*:
"At the time of sleep, however, the recitation of mantras does not yield good results.
It is stated in that very same work:
The period of sleep is the flow through the left [channel], and awakening is the flow through the right;
for the Saumya-mantra of the Manu Āntreya, it is the reverse of this.
One should know the time of awakening for both of these as well.
The winds are devoid of activity;
those from the south-east are impelled by the clouds, while those from the north are predominantly lunar and full of nectar.
As it is said in the *Svatantra-tantra*:
"O Goddess, the Vidyās are considered to have you as their essence, and the Mantras have me as their essence.
Thus, the Mantras are fiery (āgneya), while the Vidyās are lunar (saumya)."
Now, another secret: if, in rites such as pacification (*śāntika*), the wind [element] should be contrary, then the application of short and long vowels must be made in the mantra.
When the wind blows from the left, then the long [measure] of a yojana is applied;
when the wind blows from the right, then the short [measure] is applied.

"When the wind abides in both, then it is of a dual nature"—thus say the venerable feet of Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka. The meaning of this is as follows: when there is a connection with a long vowel at the beginning of a mantra and so forth, one should know that the wind is in the left arm; likewise, from a connection with short vowels, [the wind is in the right], due to the connection with short vowels.

When there is a connection with the long [vowel], it is *vāmavaha* (flowing to the left); when there is a connection with the short [vowel] of both the mantra and the vidyā, then that wind belongs to both. As for the *pallava* (sprout), as stated in the *Svatantra-tantra*:
"In the beginning there should be *yoga*, at the end the *pallava*, and in the middle the *sampuṭa*."
The first [verse] is separated by one [verse]; Vidarbha is separated by two.

The meaning of this is as follows: by the verse beginning with "First, yoga," [the author] teaches the method of application (*yojanā*) for the rites to be accomplished (*sādhya-karman*) within the mantras. This is what is being said: the term "yoga" refers to the application of the rites of the goal and the means at the beginning of the mantra and the *vidyā*. At the end of the mantra and the *vidyā*, as previously stated...
The term *yojana* refers to the "sprout" (*pallava*). The term *sampuṭa* (encasement) refers to the aforementioned joining at the beginning and end of both the mantra and the vidyā.

The term *grathana* (stringing together) refers to the mutual joining of the mantra, the vidyā, and the previously mentioned [elements], one syllable at a time. [This applies to] the mantra, the vidyā, and the previously mentioned...
The term *vidarbha* (interlacing) is derived from the joining of two syllables at a time. It is of three kinds:
one method is to insert a single syllable of the *sādhya* (the object to be accomplished) between every two syllables of the mantra;
another is to insert a single syllable of the mantra or other [elements] between every two syllables of the *sādhya*.
The supreme practitioner should join two syllables of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth between every two syllables of the mantra and the rest.
Thus it is threefold, according to the venerable Subhagānanda-pāda. An example of the conjunction with seed-syllables (*bīja*) is as stated in the *Vimalātantra*:
The Praṇava, the Goddess Mātṛkā, and Hṛllekhā constitute the two nectars;
through the union of these three nectars, even a corrupted mantra attains success.

Regarding the conjunction of the seed-syllable (*bījasaṃyoga*), it is the recitation performed seven times at the beginning of the mantra and so forth. Thereafter, the "conjunction of states" (*bhāvasaṃyoga*)—meaning "just as it is"—is to be understood from the chapter on the determination of states (*bhāvanirṇaya*). This secret practice is supreme for men; for women, it is found in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
The rule is to be understood as applying to men, and never in any way to women;
[for them], it may be anything whatsoever, by whatever means, at all times, and from any source whatsoever.
Through the yoga of meditation upon women, accomplishments will surely arise; there is no doubt,
just as a mountain of stone is pierced in secret by the mere presence of a magnet.
Just as it flows out by itself through the power of the sun,
or just as the sun-crystal clearly shines forth by the rays of the moon.
Just as water melts iron ore during the rains, so too the earth,
heated by the sun and filled with moisture, is said to release its essence through the sprinkling of water.
Just as one afflicted by hunger becomes satisfied by drinking milk,
so too does the Kula deity become well-pleased by the offering of flowers according to one's capacity.
Just as the perfection of mantra is attained through the sole service of the Guru;
just as one becomes a lord of yogis by meditating on Mahāpārvatī;
and just as enjoyment and liberation are attained merely by meditating on Tripurā.
Just as one becomes a master of spiritual accomplishments through the grace of Mahādurgā,
so too does one become free from sin merely by the remembrance of Gaṅgā.
Just as Śiva himself is produced by the mere act of attraction,
so too does this bestower of boons arise by the mere thought of the woman;
therefore, with every effort, one should initiate one's own Kaulika consort.
(Likewise, in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*): "From association with those of the family who are uninitiated, there is a loss of accomplishment at every step."
Thus ends the sixth chapter, concerning the investigation of the secret.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Now, the worship of the Kumārī. In the Jñānārṇava:
"Without the worship of the Kumārī, the entire ritual beginning with *hāṃ* and so forth will not yield its full fruit; it becomes fruitful only through her worship."

In this way, one should worship either a *suvāsinī* or a maiden for the sake of accomplishing all goals. As it is stated in the *Pañcamakrama*: "One should bring a maiden, a young girl (*kumārī*), or a *suvāsinī* who is suitable."
O Pārvatī, abandon your doubt; in the ocean of knowledge, the young wife is mature with passion.
The characteristics of the maiden are described in the Rudrajāmala:
"I shall tell [them], there is no doubt; the worship of the maiden is auspicious.
By the mere worship of her, the worship of the three worlds is accomplished."
O Lord, you are the maiden; indeed, I am you, established in a threefold form:
the supreme (parā), the lower (aparā), and the third, which is both supreme and lower (parāparā).
At that time, when there was nothing at all—neither gods, asuras, nor great serpents—I, you, and this maiden had not yet been born; [only] the three worlds existed.
The primordial creator of the world, who is directly perceived by the Yātus, is threefold;
she, Umā, has become a digit (kalā) in the form of creation for the sake of Bhava’s welfare.
At one year she becomes Sandhā; at two years, Sarasvatī;
at three years, the triple-formed Mūrti; and at four years, Kālikā.
At five years she becomes Subhagā; at six years she becomes Umā;
at seven she is Mālinī herself; and at eight years she becomes Kubjikā.
With nine [arrows] she is Kālasaṅkarṣā, and with ten she is Aparājitā.
In the eleventh year, however, she is Rudrāṇī; in the twelfth year, she is Bhairavī.
In the thirteenth [chapter], Mahālakṣmī and the fourteen Pīṭhanāyikās are described.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is considered to be the sixteenth [deity] along with the fifteen [others], including Carcikā;
thus one should worship them in this sequence until no more flowers remain.

One should worship those goddesses from the first day (pratipad) until the full moon (pūrṇā), according to the distinctions of their increasing power; especially on the great festival days (mahāparvan) and particularly during the Pavitraka rite.
O Goddess of gods, on the Mahānavamī day, one should worship the Kumārīs.
He who, being devoted, worships Piṅgalā with the sixteen [upacāras],
shall, having worshipped her with devotion, possess all prosperity.
One should worship Ekāmbā, the bearer of the Kula, among the Kula-vidyās.
Thus, one should worship the body of Consciousness through the yoga of the Praṇavas.
Aiṃ, Hrīṃ, Śrīṃ, Hrīṃ, Hūṃ—these are the five Praṇavas. Likewise, in the Rudrayāmala it is said:
"Then [there are] Vāṇī, Māyā, Lakṣmī, Māyā, and two Kūrca-s."
And these *praṇavas* are to be known for the complete worship of the Virgin Goddess.
The fourteenth vowel (au) joined with the syllables Bhrigu (b), Vindu (m),
and Indu (u) is declared to be the seed-syllable of consciousness, which bestows prosperity upon practitioners.
Hesau; Caitanyabīja (the seed of consciousness) and both Bījākṣaras (seed-syllables) are Śiva.
Thus, [they may be combined] by two, three, seven, eight, or nine [times] again.
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship them according to the rules through the daily ritual sequence;
when worshipped, they destroy obstacles as well as most formidable enemies.
Diseases, all portents of death, and ill omens are brought to an end;
the planets, yakṣas, bhūtas, vetālas, and serpents go to their destruction.
O Lord of the Kula, there are asuras, hidden beings, pretas, yoginīs, guhas, and ḍākinīs; there are great terrors, famines, and portents.
Indeed, bad dreams, untimely death, and whatever other calamities may arise,
do not prevail over him solely through the worship of Kumārī.
The supernatural powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā), as well as the underworld, pills, and gold, are accomplished;
through the worship of the Virgin Goddess, one becomes a visible divine vetāla.
Water should be offered with the syllable *aiṃ*; purification of the feet is performed with *hrīṃ* and *ukāra*;
one should offer the *arghya* with the syllable *śrīṃ*, and sandalwood paste with the *kūrca* seed-syllable.
One should offer flowers with the *śakti*-seed syllable and incense in the sixth [offering].

*Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrauṃ heṃ kulakumārike hṛdayāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the Heart, O Kulakumārikā). *Haiṃ vaiṃ hraḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ svāhā śirase svāhā* (Svāhā to the Head, Svāhā). *Aṃ hriṃ seṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* (Vaṣaṭ to the Crest-lock). *Aiṃ kula kulavāgīśvara* (O Kula, O Kulavāgīśvara).

Vāgīśvari, *huṃ* for the armor; *hrīḥ*, *phaṭ* for the weapon. *Aiṃ*: salutation to Siddhajayā, the eastern face. *Aṃ aiṃ*: salutation to Jayā, the northern face. *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*: salutation to Kubjikā, the western face. *Aiṃ*: salutation to Kālikā, the southern face.
Through the *vāgbhava* [syllable], there is agitation of form; through the *māyābīja*, the eight qualities;
through the seed-syllable of Śrī, the attainment of prosperity; and through the *hrīḥ*-seed syllable, the destruction of enemies.
By means of the seed-syllable Bhairava, one attains flight through the immortals and other such powers;
O Lord, I am always a maiden, and you too are a maiden.
One should worship either one hundred and eight or even a single maiden;
when worshipped, they respond with worship, but if treated with contempt, they burn one down.
The maiden is the Yoginī manifest; the maiden is all the deities.
She alone is the embodiment of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, worshipped by the triad of maidens.
The asuras and wicked nāgas, these malevolent grahas as well,
the bhūtas, vetālas, gandharvas, ḍākinīs, yakṣas, and rākṣasas—
All the deities are within the heart, as are Bhūr, Bhuvar, Svar, and the Bhairavas;
all elements beginning with earth, and the entire universe with its moving and non-moving beings.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
may they, being satisfied and all-pleased, come to her who worships the maiden.
Likewise, it is established therefrom Gaurī up to Kālāgniśiva;
as well as the seven continents, the oceans, and the fourteen worlds.
One should feed a young girl according to the prescribed rite and also a single Bhairavī;
likewise, one should offer water for the feet, water for the mouth, incense, saffron, and auspicious sandalwood.
Having worshipped with a spirit of devotion, one should offer everything to her;
one should perform three circumambulations—at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end.
Thereafter, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of silver, gold, and pearls should be given;
he himself shall marry the maiden, and the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā) is destroyed.
The killing of a cow, the killing of a woman, and every sin whatsoever are destroyed;
likewise, one's mothers, fathers, and brothers from all sides [are purified].
Furthermore, whoever should perform the gift of a maiden in this manner will obtain the fruit of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as good fortune and all forms of prosperity.
The blessed three-eyed Hara shall dwell eternally in the world of Rudra;
he obtains the fruit of sixty thousand times ten million horse sacrifices.
O Lord of Men, he who marries off a maiden shall obtain this fruit in embodied form for as many years as there are grains of sand in the ocean.
Having rescued each family one by one, even though he has gone to a realm resembling heaven,
those gods enjoy their pleasures for as long as the earth endures;
and the gift of a daughter is a great gift, the most excellent among all gifts.
Misfortune is swiftly destroyed, and good fortune begins to prevail.
That man shall receive honor at the royal gate and become personally esteemed by the king;
furthermore, he should diligently worship all the young maidens.
When great danger has arisen, one should worship the Kranyaka;
at that very moment, one obtains liberation—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Bhairava.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Determination of the Reality of the Virgin, in the *Tārārahasya*.
The Eighth Chapter.
Now, the most secret *puraścaraṇa* ritual is being written.
And so, in the *Gāndharva*, the Goddess said:
"O God, the *Mahācīnakrama* has been indicated, but not revealed."
"Tell me, O Mahādeva, that which bestows all great accomplishments.
Bhairava said:
"It is the direct bestower of all accomplishments, saluted by all the gods."
O Goddess, it removes all sins and destroys all diseases.
O lady of noble nature, [you shall be the mother] of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as of all the guardians of the directions,
the Bhairavas, the Gandharvas, and the Yogins.
O Goddess, it bestows the accomplishment of happiness, the great abode of all,
the remover of all sins, and the powerful Vīrasādhana.

O Maheśānī, for their sake— the one of great strength, the one of great intellect, the one of great courage, the pure one, the one who is greatly translucent, the one possessed of splendor, and the one devoted to the welfare of all beings— this Vīrasādhana has been described.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights—
and especially during the dark fortnight— one should accomplish one's desired goal by means of this [mantra].
O noble lady, when the night of Tuesday has passed into its third watch,
at the midpoint of that half-watch, one should properly prepare the articles for worship and the sacrificial offering (bali).
Meat with sauce, molasses, goat meat, liquor, flour-cakes, and milk-rice.
And there should be various fruits as an offering (naivedya), prepared according to the specific rites prescribed in their respective tantras.
Having brought the site of the funeral pyre together with friends who hold sharp weapons in their hands—
friends endowed with equal virtues— the practitioner himself, free from fear, [proceeds].
The characteristics of the cremation ground (*citā*) are as follows:
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cremation ground is not associated with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
having reached it among places such as those of the *caṇḍālas*, it grants success solely and swiftly.
Also in the Vīratantra:
"Having taken either a corpse or a funeral pyre, having gone there as one pleases,
and having bathed and established a firm protection, one should be intent upon meditation on the deity."
If the practitioner is afraid there, other practitioners in the four directions will repeatedly roar like heroes with the words, "Do not come here!"
If this Bhairava is not proclaimed as being alone by himself,
he is adorned with garments, ornaments, and decorations, and faces the east.
One should sprinkle the sacrificial grounds with the Astra-mantra and the root-mantra,
while meditating upon the dust from the feet of the Guru, as well as Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka.
Having first honored the Yoginī and Mātṛkā with his left foot,
[he addressed] those gods and terrifying Rākṣasas who were stationed there.
Piśācas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, and Gandharvas, as well as women who roam the sky.
They shall grant you success here and likewise be the protectors of me.
Having prostrated with this mantra, one should offer three handfuls of flowers to the Lord of the Cremation Ground,
Bhairava Kālabhairava.

One who knows the mantras should worship Mahākāla with effort in the four directions beginning with the east, using water for the feet and other offerings; thereafter, one should present the bali offering.
Following that, one should [place] the seed-syllable of sound (Ś) and then the lord of the cremation ground (KṢ).
"O Lord,
accept this offering of impure food at the end; thereafter,
cause the pair of feet to accept it, which wards off all obstacles."
"Grant me success thereafter, accompanied by svāhā.
With this mantra beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava), the first bali offering is prescribed.
After Māyānta and Bhairava, and thereafter Bhayānaka,
having extracted the mantra as before, one should offer the bali-oblation in the south.
And in the *hūm*-mantra, one should extract [the name] after Mahākāla as before;
in the west, one should offer it to Kāla-deva with the *praṇava* at the beginning.
At the end of the word "śabda," at the end of the word "kāla," and then after "bhairava," one should likewise remove [the syllables] "śmaśānādhipa" as before in the north.
Then, in the midst of the funeral pyre, one should offer three supreme oblations [with the mantra]:
"O Kālarātri, Mahākālī, Kālikā of terrible sound!"
"O Mother, bring this offering to the house; grant me supreme accomplishment.
Having given the offering to Kālikā, one should cause it to be given to Bhūtanātha.
At the end of the word "śabda," one should offer the supreme bali-oblation with the mantra beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ), which includes the words "bhūtanāthāya" and "śmaśānādhipa."
At the end of the syllable *hūṃ*, and at the end of "Lord of all the hosts" (*sarvagaṇanātha*), one should append "to the Overlord" (*adhipāya*);
having placed this at the head of the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), one should extract it as before.

O beautiful one, having offered the bali-oblation with the mantra beginning with "Tārā," and having sprinkled the bones with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should then write the pīṭha-mantra.
One should place the mantra upon a seat made of either birch bark or a banyan leaf.
Having spread a seat upon that [ground] and then assumed the vīrāsana posture there,
O Goddess of gods, one should arrange the protection of the directions with half of the vīra-mantra.
O Goddess, after the two seed-syllables of the *kūrca* and the pair of *māyā*, [there are]:
"Kālike, Ghoradaṃṣṭre, Pracaṇḍe, Caṇḍanāyike."
Having uttered "dāraya" twice to split the Dānavas, then "hana" twice; then [utter] "chedaya" twice to cut the corpse-body, the great obstacle.
Ending with *dviṭha*, ending with *varma* and *śastra*, and ending with *vīra*—these are considered the half-mantras.
One should scatter clods of earth consecrated with this mantra in the ten directions;
in their midst, Bhairava and the Goddess are not overcome by obstacles.
O Goddess of gods, if through negligence the practitioner becomes overwhelmed by fear,
he will not be overcome there if he is protected by those various groups of friends.

Having prepared a wick from the fibers of the *arka*, *indrasita*, and *vāṭyālata* plants according to the prescribed proportions, one should place a lamp there and worship the Weapon-mantra (*astra*) therein.
When that great lamp has been overcome by obstacles,
one should write the Kulapradīpikā mantra beneath it with the Astra-mantra.
One should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other rites according to the procedure prescribed for that particular Kalpa;
thereafter, one should install the Vidyā conjoined with the letters of the Mātṛkā upon the six limbs.
Tārā is proclaimed to be sixfold through the yoga of sequential progression.
One who has performed the sixfold placement upon the body becomes the Lord of the Universe himself.
Having performed either the sixfold placement or the placement of Tāraka, one should then worship her.
Having become intent upon mantra and meditation, one should recite the mantra with a mind focused on nothing else.
If it consists of a single syllable, one should recite it a thousand times;
for a two-syllable mantra, eight thousand times; and for a three-syllable mantra, fifty thousand times.
Thereafter, however, the knower of mantras [performed] one thousand half-elephants.
Alternatively: "Having begun the recitation at night, one should perform it until sunrise;
having offered the bali-offering at the beginning of the recitation, one should offer the bali-offering again afterwards."
Whether at the end of the recitation or during the recitation, if the words "Give!
Give! are spoken, then one should also offer a bali-oblation consisting of either a buffalo or a goat.
There is no looking about in any direction, nor is there reunion with kinsmen;
likewise, there is [no escape] from water and other difficult terrains, from serpents, fire, elephants, and fanged beasts.
Whatever resides in the minds of birds, insects, and spirits—
all that, having understood it to be like a dream, one should avoid everywhere with fearlessness.
O Goddess, having completed the ritual practice, one should cause the preceptor, the preceptor’s son, or the preceptor’s wife to receive a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's means.
For one who has correctly mastered even a single mantra, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished anywhere; what need is there to speak of a man who possesses many mantras? He is Śiva himself.
Since, O Goddess of the Gods, the worship of the Guru is most weighty in all circumstances,
one should never engage in the discussion of mantras and tantras in his presence.
When the feet of the Guru are indeed worshipped, all the gods become happy;
for that Sadāśiva is the father of all mantras and tantras.
O Goddess, service to another is one thing, and the glorification of another deity is quite another;
without the Guru as one's God, one goes to hell in his presence.
If one should be mounted upon a corpse, that specific procedure is stated here:
[it should be done] in a dry house, at the root of a bilva tree, on a riverbank, or at a crossroads.
Having led [the deity] especially to a cremation ground, one should lift it up and adorn it;
having brought it back, one should first establish it and perform the entire network of ritual placements (*nyāsa*).
Then, having inscribed the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamantra*), one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having worshipped and offered a seat, one should perform protection for oneself;
then, according to the rule, one should perform the satiation of the deity within the mouth of the corpse.

Then, having recited all the mantras, one shall become a master of all accomplishments (siddhi). One should utter the mantra beginning with the sound "Tāra" (Om) and ending with "namo" directed toward the corpse.
This is the mantra for the corpse's sleep; then follows the mantra for the corpse's seat.
At the end of the mantra, there should be Bhuvaneśī, ending with *phaṭ*; thus the mantra is declared.
O Goddess, this Mahānīla-krama bestows all accomplishments;
it must not be spoken of to anyone, but kept secret for my pleasure.
It is [the means] for the heroic practice (*vīrasādhana*) regarding all living beings who have lost their lives.
O Hero, having discarded the *brāhmaṇa* and the cow-dung, one should accomplish the *sādhana*.
O beloved, great corpses are praised as the most excellent means for accomplishment;
having abandoned a Brahmin woman, O hero, one should accomplish the heroic sādhana.
The *kṣudrā* [mantras] are recommended for practitioners to achieve all accomplishments;
however, O Goddess, the *puraścaryā* performed in a cremation ground is said to be difficult to attain.

Now, that which was spoken in the Bhairavatantra regarding the procedure for attaining the siddhi of the heroes— which is concealed in all tantras within the Bhāvasarvasva— was taught by Śambhu, the God of gods.
By the mere knowledge of which even one of meager fortune attains success;
in a period of a single day and night, the best of practitioners achieves it with ease.
Having received the mantra from the presence of the guru, being devoted solely to the service of the guru,
one should diligently understand the mantra’s ears, mouth, eyes, and vital breaths.
Having understood the mantra and the ritual pin (kīlaka), one should perform the preliminary service of the mantra;
once perfected through the fulfillment of the preparatory rites, one should practice for heroic accomplishment (vīrasiddhi).
Thus it is said in the *Svacchandabhairava* as well: "Even with thorough exertion, the desired accomplishment does not arise;
in that case, the practitioner must perform the *vīrasādhana*."
Free from attachment and greed for sons, wife, and wealth, and devoid of delusion,
I shall either accomplish the mantra or cast off this body.
Having made such a vow, one should contemplate the sacrificial materials;
whatever material belongs to which mantra, that very thing should be accepted by the practitioners.
An example of the variegated characteristic (*śavalakṣaṇa*) is as follows:
"In the performance of the Heroic Sadhana (*vīrasādhana*), for all living beings devoid of life,
one should perform the Heroic Sadhana having set aside a Brahmin or a cow corpse."
Great corpses are praised when the primary heroic accomplishment (vīrasādhana) is to be performed;
however, a Brahmin, having abandoned a woman, should accomplish the heroic accomplishment.
Therefore, for those performing the ritual application, [the following] are recommended for the attainment of all success:
one who is more than two years old, or five, or if they are young.
A fetus from the seventh or eighth month, or a corpse,
or a Cāṇḍāla who has been struck down, bestows the fruit of swift accomplishment.
Thus, in the *Kṣetramāra* and also in the *Bhairavatantra*, it is said that [the corpse] should be pierced with a staff and so forth, and having been overcome and deceased in water,
[one should bring] the corpse; one should not take a corpse that has died by its own will.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-performance even in rites such as the Aśvamedha.
However, some [hold that] if a cognition arises regarding the killing of a Śyena bird as being an object of intense aversion, then...

The Śyena sacrifice is to be performed; it is the same here as well. If one wishes to act by way of many paths, then non-association with those [paths] must be practiced, because otherwise, by seeking out the path of the Guru, he remains on the pure path everywhere. That has been explained regarding the animal sacrifice, since there is heard an explanatory passage (arthavāda) of censure regarding that very point.

This has been stated; however, it is not so in this case. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-performance regarding the killing of a newborn and other such acts prescribed [elsewhere].

As for the search for the path of the Guru, that is for the purpose of making known the family custom (*kulācāra*), because it is understood as such by the scriptural statement (*vacana*). For example, for some, there is the worship of the *sūtikā* (the woman who has recently given birth) on the sixth day.

Regarding the statement "for some, on the twenty-first day," if there is no fault [in the timing], one should not speak otherwise; for just as there might be a reversal of that [order] out of fear of violating family tradition when no fault exists, so it is here as well. Having reflected thus, the sprouting of the explanation of the intention of Maheśa’s heart must be articulated by those following the Śākta, Śaiva, and Vaiṣṇava traditions. 3.

Now, one might ask: what would be the purpose of that injunction? To this he says, "The bank-path," and so forth. O Mother, having known the bank-path in its true nature, he performs a libation with the waters of the sacred sites—that is, with showers of nectar—in his own ground, the thousand-petalled [lotus], which is immeasurable because it is the most excellent; thus, he brings about satisfaction.

Having worshipped with mental perfumes and other offerings, and having meditated upon the form of the young woman, one should proceed through the sequence of ascending and descending to fashion the *cakra* according to the sequence of the *Kulakuṇḍalinī* to be described; then, having fully worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings,
if one performs libations with divine substances, one becomes a partaker of the fruit to be described.
But the property of the gods belongs to Kubjikā.
